transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE); Anita Kapoor (Stratus AI - VP ML); Evan Liu (SRE); Marco Diaz (ML Eng)
Notes/Shared links: Redwood deck (link), benchmark spreadsheet (link), SOC2 + VPC doc (link)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick discovery to understand Stratus AI's latency and throughput targets; discuss hosted vs dedicated vs private; validate p95 targets, concurrency, streaming requirements; agree next steps for benchmark runs and pricing follow-up.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, joined by Diego our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Anita (Stratus AI): Hi, good thanks. Busy week but excited to talk through this.
[00:11] Evan (SRE): Morning/afternoon for some of us, thanks for making time.
[00:15] Diego (Redwood SE): Cool - quick agenda, we wanna understand your latency targets (p95), concurrency, whether you need streaming, and what your failure/cost tolerances look like. Then we'll sketch options: hosted, dedicated, private.
[00:28] Anita: Sounds good. High level: we run a chat assistant in prod used by internal and external customers. Right now it's on a hybrid infra, we have a lot of spiky traffic - during peaks we see up to 400 concurrent requests, typical sequence lengths around 150 tokens, but some long sessions go to 1k. Our SLOs are p95 generation latency under 400ms end-to-end for our customer-facing flows.
[00:50] Marco (ML Eng): To add, our token/sec expectations vary; for short prompts we want high tokens/sec to keep interactive feel; for longer batch jobs it's okay to be slower. We're curious how Redwood's batching and KV cache affect p95 for those mixed workloads.
[01:10] Diego: OK that's helpful. So 400ms p95 for 150 tokens is pretty tight. Are you measuring network+inference or just server-side inference?
[01:18] Anita: End-to-end - includes our app, network, and the model response time. So we'd like Redwood to be at most ~200-250ms server-side so we can budget client and other middleware.
[01:28] Evan: Also we need streaming responses for token-by-token earlier rendering - that reduces perceived latency. Important question: do you support partial streaming with low p95?
[01:36] Diego: Yes, Redwood supports streaming across hosted and dedicated. Streaming impacts throughput slightly because of more frequent flushes, but we have optimizations - continuous batching, low-latency kernels, and early prefix cache hits. For your 150-token median, we can often hit sub-200ms p95 on dedicated hardware depending on model size and quantization. On hosted, it depends on plan and concurrency.
[01:58] Anita: When you say model size - we're evaluating a 7B and a 13B open model. Which is realistic to keep under that p95 at 150 tokens?
[02:06] Diego: 7B is much easier. 13B is doable on dedicated with A10/A100-ish class nodes with optimized kernels and quantization; p95 will depend on batch size and concurrency. For example, on 13B we typically see 80-120 tokens/sec per GPU for long sequences, but tail latency depends on request coalescing. We'll send exact bench numbers.
[02:26] Marco: Token/sec per GPU - do you have numbers for streaming vs non-streaming? Also how does KV cache impact long sessions?
[02:32] Diego: Streaming tends to reduce aggregate tokens/sec slightly because we emit tokens earlier, but it helps perceived latency. KV cache helps for multi-turn - if prefix is cached, subsequent turns avoid full recompute and p95 drops significantly. In some internal cases we've seen p95 drop from 700ms to ~180ms for cached prefixes. But cache hit rate is workload dependent.
[02:52] Evan: Network: we need VPC peering and option for private deployment. Security is a hard requirement - SOC 2, SSO, and customer-managed KMS for keys.
[02:59] Maya: Yep - we have SOC 2 and the private Redwood offering supports VPC/no-egress and KMS/HSM integrations. We can send the SOC2 report and our VPC runbook.
[03:08] Anita: Excellent. Cost is also important. We might start on hosted to iterate, then move to dedicated as we scale. For dedicated pricing we need an estimate based on expected concurrency and tokens/sec to justify.
[03:18] Diego: Totally - for dedicated we size GPU pools based on peak concurrency and target p95. Quick rule of thumb: if you need 400 concurrent low-latency streaming sessions on 13B, you'd likely need N GPUs (we'll compute in spreadsheet). For 7B it's fewer. We'll model cost-per-token and per-hour.
[03:32] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[03:35] Marco: For the bench run, what do you need from us? We can provide traffic capture, sample prompt distributions, and a staging VPC.
[03:43] Diego: Perfect - ideally: 1) sample prompts and sequence length distribution, 2) expected concurrency distribution (p50/p95/p99), 3) a staging VPC peered or access to a test endpoint, 4) desired model and quantization preference. We'll run 3 scenarios: hosted-proxy baseline, dedicated with optimized kernels, and private (on-prem/VPC) if you want.
[04:03] Anita: We definitely want the three scenarios. Also curious about graceful degradation - if capacity is saturated does Redwood fallback to smaller model automatically?
[04:11] Diego: We support smart routing and fallbacks; you can configure policy-level fallbacks to lower-cost variants. That reduces cost and avoids total outage, though output quality can change so you'd want canaries and score-based routing.
[04:24] Evan: On SRE side, how do you expose metrics and tracing? We need per-token latency histograms, request ids, and 1s granularity metrics that integrate with our datadog.
[04:33] Maya: The Redwood console exposes per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, traces, and a metrics API. We can provide a demo of the console in the next call.
[04:43] Anita: Nice. Back to p95: our current internal infra hits p95 of ~550ms at the peak for 150 tokens. We want to get below 400ms end-to-end. If Redwood can guarantee ~200ms server-side for our median case, that's promising. Can you give realistic expectations for p95 across configurations?
[05:00] Diego: Rough baseline ballpark: Hosted (shared) on small tier - 13B might be p95 700-900ms at moderate concurrency; hosted higher tiers can be lower. Dedicated with A100 + optimized kernels + q4 quantization could be sub-200-300ms p95 for 150 tokens. 7B often hits sub-100-200ms p95. But this is workload dependent - batchiness, streaming, and cache hit rates change the tail. We'll provide a spreadsheet with calibrated numbers and a recommended pilot config.
[05:27] Marco: If we go q4 quantization, do you see any quality regressions for our LLM finetuned conversational model? We can do eval sets.
[05:35] Diego: Yes, small regressions possible; Redwood Optimize has quality monitoring and regressions alerts tied to evals/prompt sets. We recommend running your eval harness against quantized variants during the bench.
[05:48] Anita: That works. About concurrency: at 400 concurrent sessions, what's token/sec impact? If each session averages 2 tokens/sec (interactive typing), that's 800 tokens/sec sustained. How many GPUs to keep p95 under 250ms?
[06:01] Diego: Quick calc: tokens/sec per GPU varies by model and config - for 13B on A100 with q4 we might see 400-800 tokens/sec per GPU depending on seq length and batchability. For interactive sessions with small requests, we rely on continuous batching to coalesce requests. For your 800 tokens/sec steady, that could be 1-2 GPUs in ideal batching case but tail and concurrency force more headroom - we'd probably propose 2-4 GPUs as a starting point. We'll model with your actual distributions.
[06:27] Evan: We prefer headroom - we want to avoid tail spikes causing SLO breaches. How does autoscaling / burst capacity work in Dedicated?
[06:34] Diego: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity across pools. You can reserve base capacity and allow controlled bursts to shared capacity with fallbacks defined. Autoscale policies can be time-based or metric-based (p95, queue length).
[06:46] Maya: Quick note: for private on-prem, kernel selection and network topology matter more; we typically do a short site audit and a custom sizing pass.
[06:55] Anita: Got it. Any gotchas about streaming throughput we should know when modeling?
[07:00] Diego: Two things: 1) Streaming increases number of responses so overhead per request rises - it's small but multiplies at high concurrency. 2) If you rely on very small token emissions (1 token at a time), some kernels work better than others; we'll test that. Also client-side buffering can impact perceived latency.
[07:17] Marco: For the bench, can we run both streaming and non-streaming tests for the same prompt set so we can compare?
[07:22] Diego: Absolutely - we'll do paired runs. We'll also capture CPU/GPU utilization and KV cache hit metrics.
[07:28] Anita: On the security doc front, please send network architecture and how audit logs are stored. We have compliance checks that require log retention for 1 year.
[07:36] Maya: We'll send SOC2 and our audit log retentions; we can support longer retention as an add-on.
[07:41] Evan: For the benchmarking window, we'll want to run during our off-peak hours (US PST late night) - Diego, can you do that?
[07:47] Diego: Yes, we can coordinate. We'll need your staging VPC access or a short-lived hosted endpoint.
[07:51] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[07:54] Marco: A couple more technical Qs - how deterministic are your p95 numbers across regions? We have users in EU and NA and want similar tails.
[07:59] Diego: Region parity depends on underlying hardware fleet - we try to maintain similar instance types across regions, but exact p95 can vary. We'll run bench jobs in both regions and provide a regional breakdown. Also mention of routing policies: you can route by latency or cost so EU traffic stays in EU.
[08:18] Anita: Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[08:21] Maya: I'll capture next steps: send benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 + VPC runbook, sample configs; Diego will coordinate bench run and prepare recommended dedicated sizing and cost model.
[08:31] Anita: And we'll send sample prompts and traffic profile.
[08:34] Evan: One last ask - can you show us a past benchmark with similar scale (400 concurrency) even if anonymized?
[08:39] Diego: Yes, we'll include an anonymized case study in the docs.
[08:43] Marco: Sounds good.
[08:45] Speaker 3: (laughter)
[08:47] Maya: Okay we are at about 45 minutes in - any final questions?
[08:50] Anita: Nothing else on my side. Thanks - looking forward to the spreadsheet.
[08:54] Evan: Thanks, appreciate it.
[08:55] Diego: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up and schedule the benchmark window.
